state.misconception_label: Has used slant height and base to find area of a triangle rather than perpendicular height and base

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: How would you calculate the area of this triangle? ![A triangle, base 12m. All three sides are equal.](). I got \( \frac{12 \times 12}{2} \) because I added the side lengths instead of multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're building a roof for a dollhouse with a triangular shape. To find the area correctly, you need to measure the height from the peak of the roof straight down to the base, not along the slanted side. This way, you'll get the right amount of material needed to cover the roof.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see! So I need to measure the height straight down from the top to the base instead of using the slanted side. But how do I find that height if I only know the sides of the triangle?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're playing a game of hide and seek with your friends in a park. To find someone hiding behind a tree, you wouldn't run straight towards the tree at an angle, right? You would walk directly towards the tree to reach them. In the same way, to find the height of the triangle, you need to draw a line straight down from the top to the base. This will give you the perpendicular height you need to calculate the area correctly.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher correctly identifies the need for perpendicular height but uses vague analogies instead of addressing the student's actual question about how to calculate it, and the student's final turn shows no mathematical progress beyond restating what perpendicular means.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses real-world scenarios (dollhouse roof, hide and seek), these analogies don't actually ground the mathematical concept in concrete experience—the hide-and-seek analogy particularly fails to connect meaningfully to finding perpendicular height, and neither analogy helps the student calculate or understand how to derive the height value.
